kurz: How warrants, knock-outs, factor certificates and CFDs implement leverage, and the different ways in which losses arise with each of them.

bloecke.md:
For most private portfolios, access to the derivatives exchange is the main hurdle. A DAX option (ODAX) is based on €5 per index point. At an index level of 26,000 points, a single contract thus controls €130,000 of notional value, and trading on Eurex requires separate approval. This gap is filled by securitised leveraged products (warrants, knock-outs and factor certificates) and, off-exchange, by the contract for difference (CFD). The securitised products can be traded from a few euros upwards and are held in the normal securities account. CFDs are not securities; they require a separate CFD trading account with the provider.

Legally, all three types of certificate are **bearer bonds** (Inhaberschuldverschreibungen), that is, payment promises of the issuing bank. They are not segregated fund assets (Sondervermögen), and there is no deposit protection and no clearing house in between. With a Eurex option, Eurex Clearing acts as the counterparty; with a warrant, the issuer alone is liable for the payment. The standard example of this is the Lehman insolvency in September 2008. Certificates defaulted at the time, regardless of how the underlying had performed, and investors only received partial payments from the insolvency proceedings years later. In response, collateralised certificates (COSI) were created, but they make up only a small part of the market.

Buyers of a leveraged certificate bear the market risk and, in addition, the [[Issuer risk|issuer risk]]. Even an accurate assessment of the market does not protect against the insolvency of the bank that issued the product.

## Warrants

A warrant securitises the same payout as an option, but in small denominations. The **ratio** indicates how much of the underlying one warrant refers to. At 0.1, it takes ten warrants to represent one share. The issuer sets the price itself, with its own assumption about implied volatility and its own bid-ask spread. Although the warrants are traded on the stock exchange, the issuer itself acts as market maker there. Investors cannot become option writers themselves; they can only buy what the bank offers.

Two leverage terms are often confused. *Simple leverage* is a purely arithmetical figure. It indicates how much of the underlying you control per euro invested, but says nothing about how the warrant reacts to price movements. That is shown by **[[Omega|omega]]**, also called effective leverage. It is simple leverage multiplied by delta. Only omega indicates by what percentage the warrant rises when the underlying rises by 1%. Even that applies only to a small movement in the next moment and with volatility otherwise unchanged.

bloecke.formel: Simple leverage = (S × ratio) / P        Omega = Delta × simple leverage        Premium (call) = (K + P/ratio − S) / S
bloecke.erklaerung: The premium (Aufgeld) indicates how much the underlying must rise by maturity for the buyer to reach break-even. Of the individual figures on a warrant's data sheet, it is the most meaningful.
variablen: price sensitivity of the option, between 0 and 1 for a call

bloecke.md:
Illustrative calculation using Black-Scholes: underlying €100, call warrant with a strike price of €110, six months to expiry, ratio 0.1, implied volatility 28%, interest rate 2%. The fair value is €0.45, and the issuer quotes an ask price of €0.47. The warrant is bought at €0.47.

The break-even at maturity is €114.70. The underlying must therefore rise by almost 15% in half a year for the buyer not to lose money. The following values are model prices excluding the bid-ask spread on sale, which costs around another 2%.

bloecke.titel: Result of the warrant compared with the purchase price of €0.47
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation. In two of the four scenarios with a rising price, the warrant still ends in the red, because time value and implied volatility also influence the result.

serien.name: Change in value of the warrant

bloecke.md: The issuer bases its price on an implied volatility of its own choosing. If it falls from 28% to 24%, the warrant in the example loses around a quarter of its value, even though the underlying has not changed. Before known dates such as quarterly results or interest rate decisions, the priced-in volatility is systematically high; afterwards it declines. Buyers who get in immediately before such dates pay the highest price for the expected movement and lose money even if their forecast is correct.

## Knock-outs

Depending on the provider, knock-out products are called turbos, mini futures or something similar. They have a strike price (the financing level) and a knock-out barrier, which is often at some distance from the strike price and sometimes at the same level. Their price corresponds approximately to the intrinsic value plus a small premium: `Price (long) ≈ (S − strike price + premium) × ratio`. Knock-outs are therefore cheaper than warrants and lose hardly any time value. The drawback is a hard condition. If the price touches the barrier even for a moment, the product expires immediately. With the stop-loss variant, a residual value remains; with the classic variant, nothing. If the price recovers an hour later, that no longer helps.

The leverage is not constant, and this property of the product type is the one most often overlooked. It results from `Leverage = S / (S − strike price)` and grows as the price approaches the strike price, that is, when the position is already making a loss.

bloecke.titel: Leverage of a long knock-out with strike price and barrier at €90
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation, ratio 1, without premium. At €100 the leverage is 10, at €95 it is already 19, and at €91 it is 91. Leverage, and with it the risk, grows faster than the loss.

bloecke.md: The knock-out barrier applies throughout the entire term and, as a rule, also outside German trading hours. A single wick, that is, a brief price spike, in a low-volume night session is enough for a total loss. With open-end products, the strike price is also adjusted daily by the financing costs, so that the barrier slowly approaches the price. With a long product held for months, the distance to the barrier therefore shrinks even if nothing has changed in the market.

## Factor certificates

A factor certificate tracks a strategy index and not the underlying directly. This index multiplies the daily percentage change of the underlying relative to the previous day's close by the factor. The leverage is therefore the same again at the start of every trading day. It follows that over longer periods the product performs quite differently from the multiple of the underlying. It is **path-dependent**, meaning the result depends on the final level of the underlying and, in addition, on the path taken to get there.

bloecke.titel: Six days of alternating +10% and −10% (factor 2, excluding costs)
Underlying and factor 2 certificate over six trading days
bloecke.unter: Teaching example without costs. The underlying loses 2.97%, the certificate 11.53% instead of the 5.94% expected from simple doubling. The difference of 5.6 percentage points arises solely from the fluctuations.

bloecke.md:
This effect is called **[[Beta slippage|beta slippage]]**. It is an inevitable consequence of the daily adjustment and not a design flaw. It occurs in every volatile sideways market, with long and short factor certificates alike. In addition, there are financing costs and an annual management fee. Factor certificates are therefore intended for holding periods of days and not of years. They are unsuitable as a convenient way to hold permanent leverage on an index.

## CFDs

The contract for difference is an over-the-counter contract with the provider and not a securitised instrument. Only the price difference is settled. Under ESMA's product intervention measures of 27 March 2018, the following apply to retail clients in the EU: fixed leverage limits, an obligation to close out at 50% of the required minimum margin, negative balance protection per account, a ban on bonuses and a standardised risk warning. In this warning, every provider must disclose the proportion of its retail clients who lose money, typically 70% to 85%. In Germany, BaFin (Federal Financial Supervisory Authority) had already ruled out the obligation to make additional payments (Nachschusspflicht) for private investors in 2017 and made the rules permanent in 2019.

bloecke.titel: ESMA leverage limits for retail clients and the resulting price buffer

bloecke.md: The last column is our own calculation. It shows how far the price may move against the position before half of the minimum margin is used up and the provider must close out. This assumes that there is no further balance in the account. For major currency pairs, that is 1.67%. A movement of this size is rare on a single day, but common within a few weeks. [[Negative balance protection]] prevents you from losing more than the account balance. It does not prevent the rapid loss of the entire account balance. On top of this come financing costs for every position held overnight, as well as the spread, which the provider sets itself.

bloecke.md:
## Tax

Gains from these products are income from capital assets. They are subject to 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer), plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge on the tax and, where applicable, church tax. Before that, the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 per person is deducted (Section 20(9) EStG, Income Tax Act). Depending on the structure, the applicable provision is Section 20(2) sentence 1 no. 3 EStG for a derivative transaction (Termingeschäft) with cash settlement, or no. 7 for the sale of another capital claim. In practice, the custodian bank takes care of the classification.

On the loss side, this distinction has hardly mattered since the Annual Tax Act 2024 (Jahressteuergesetz) of 2 December 2024. The former limit of €20,000 a year for offsetting losses from derivative transactions and from bad debts was abolished without replacement and, under Section 52(28) EStG, no longer applies in any open cases. Older guides that still mention this limit are out of date. Losses from warrants, knock-outs, factor certificates and CFDs therefore go into the general “Other” loss pot (allgemeiner Verlusttopf). A separate pot now exists only for shares. Losses from the sale of shares may only be offset against gains from share sales (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG). This restriction does not apply the other way round, so losses from the general pot may also reduce gains on shares. The basic rule still applies that capital losses may not be offset against wages, rent or business income and can only be carried forward (Section 20(6) sentence 1 EStG).

- Read the key information document before every purchase. It states the ratio, the barrier and the costs. The issuer gives the premium and implied volatility on the product page.
- Never order “at best”. The issuer sets the price, and outside Xetra core trading hours the spread is wider.
- When comparing two seemingly identical warrants, look at the implied volatility and not at the price. The issuer determines its earnings through the level of volatility it applies.
- Choose the position size so that a total loss is bearable. With leveraged products, it is a frequent outcome and not a fringe scenario.

As a rule, issuers do not bet against their customers. An issuer that sells warrants hedges the position on the derivatives market (delta hedging). It earns from the bid-ask spread, the premium and the difference between the volatility it applies when selling and the volatility at which it hedges itself. It does not earn from the customer's loss. This argument is less reassuring than it first appears, however. The conflict of interest does not disappear as a result; it shifts from the direction of the market to the pricing. The issuer must disclose the costs contained in the pricing in the key information document as total costs in euros and as a percentage.

mitnehmen: Warrants, knock-outs, factor certificates and CFDs leverage the same underlying, but losses arise with them through four different mechanisms: time value, barrier, path dependency and margin.
Certificates are debt securities without deposit protection, so if the issuer becomes insolvent, even a product showing a profit faces a partial or total loss.
The leverage of a knock-out rises the closer the price gets to the barrier, and is therefore greatest where the risk is also greatest.
Factor certificates lose money in volatile sideways markets even if the underlying ends up unchanged, and are therefore instruments for holding periods of days.

Since the Annual Tax Act 2024 (JStG 2024), the €20,000 limit for losses from derivative transactions no longer applies; these losses go into the general loss pot but remain blocked against other types of income.

begriffe.text: Effective leverage of an option or a warrant, calculated as simple leverage times delta. Omega indicates by what percentage the instrument responds to a 1% movement in the underlying.
Percentage premium that the underlying must make up by maturity for the buyer of a warrant to reach break-even.
Price threshold at which a leveraged certificate expires immediately and permanently as soon as it is touched. It applies throughout the entire term, usually also outside German trading hours.
Systematic loss of value of a factor certificate in volatile sideways markets. It arises because the leverage is recalculated every day on the basis of the previous day's close.
Default risk of the bank that issued a certificate or a warrant. These products are bearer bonds (Inhaberschuldverschreibungen) without deposit protection.
EU requirement for retail clients' CFD accounts under which the loss is limited to the account balance. There is no obligation to make additional payments.
